strengths: The paper presents a unified feed-forward model for multiple 3D tasks, including point map reconstruction, camera pose estimation, depth estimation, surface normal prediction, and novel view synthesis, which is a useful step toward general-purpose 3D reconstruction.

The multi-modal prior prompting mechanism is well motivated and technically sensible: compact camera/intrinsic tokens are concatenated, dense depth tokens are added, and dynamic prior injection during training enables flexible inference with arbitrary prior subsets.

The empirical evaluation is extensive, covering multiple benchmarks and comparing against strong recent baselines such as VGGT, π3, StableNormal, GeoWizard, FLARE, and AnySplat. The no-prior WorldMirror already surpasses VGGT and π3 on point map reconstruction, and prior combinations yield substantial further gains.

Ablations on prior embedding choices (single token vs. dense Plücker/raymap) and on NVS components (GT cameras, novel-view supervision, GS DPT head) provide useful insights, even if some are imperfect.
The paper includes qualitative visualizations across in-the-wild images and AI-generated videos, demonstrating generalization beyond standard benchmarks.
Limitations are acknowledged in the appendix, including poor performance on dynamic scenes and autonomous driving data, as well as constraints on input resolution and number of views.
The surface normal results are strong across ScanNet, NYUv2, and iBims-1, showing that the multi-task framework can outperform specialized normal estimation methods.
weaknesses: A central claim of pose-free novel view synthesis is not supported by the main method description: Eq. 4 states that Gaussian centers are obtained by back-projecting predicted depth using ground-truth camera poses and intrinsics. The main NVS results therefore appear to use privileged ground-truth camera information, making comparisons to pose-free methods like AnySplat unfair. Although the ablation 'w/o GT Cameras' shows only a small drop, the headline numbers in Table 4 are likely not pose-free, which undermines the claimed contribution.

Eq. 11 for the gradient consistency loss is written as \|\nabla\hat{D}_i[\hat{M}_i]-\nabla\hat{D}_i[\hat{M}_i]\|, which is identically zero. The text says it should enforce consistency between the GS-rendered depth map and the depth-head pseudo depth, but the equation does not distinguish these two quantities. As written, the loss is meaningless and the implementation is unclear.

Reproducibility is limited: code and models are stated to be 'publicly available soon,' but no code, weights, or exact data splits are provided. Training uses 32 H20 GPUs with 15 datasets, and important details such as random seeds, full preprocessing, and exact evaluation protocols for all tasks are incomplete. This makes it difficult for others to reliably build on the work.

The reference list contains numerous citation errors and inconsistencies, e.g., 'Huang et al. (2024)' for DeepMVS (2018), 'Ji and Jones (2025)' for Jang et al., 'Jensen and Jensen (2023)' for Jensen et al. (2014), and 'Kar et al. (2023)' for a 2022 paper. These errors reduce confidence in the paper's overall care and reliability.

The paper overclaims 'universal' and 'any-prior' capabilities. The supported priors are limited to camera pose, calibrated intrinsics, and depth; no other modalities are explored. Missing or invalid priors are handled simply by zeroing tokens, with no analysis of robustness to noisy or incorrect priors.

The curriculum learning strategy is described but not systematically ablated. The paper does not isolate the contribution of task sequencing, data scheduling, or progressive resolution, so it is unclear which components are essential versus incidental.

The depth prior used in point map reconstruction may come from ground-truth sensor depth in benchmark evaluations. This is a privileged input not always available in real applications, and the paper does not adequately discuss how such priors would be obtained in practice or how sensitive results are to their quality.
The efficiency claim is not fully substantiated: inference time is only partially reported, and the computational cost of the multi-task model and training procedure is not thoroughly analyzed.

The paper does not discuss the ground-truth camera reliance in NVS as a limitation, despite it being a potential issue for the claimed pose-free setting. This omission weakens the honesty of the limitations discussion.

strengths: The paper presents a genuinely broad and coherent system: a single feed-forward model that accepts optional geometric priors (intrinsics, camera poses, depth) and simultaneously outputs point maps, cameras, depth, surface normals, and 3D Gaussians. This unification of prior-conditioning and multi-task geometry prediction is a useful direction.

The prior-guidance evaluation is reasonably systematic. Tables 1 and 4 and Figure 6 show, across several configurations, that a single prior improves not only its own task but also other tasks, which supports the central claim that multi-modal priors act synergistically.

Quantitative results are strong on several benchmarks: point-map reconstruction improves over VGGT and pi3 on 7-Scenes/NRGBD/DTU (e.g., mean Acc 0.043 vs 0.046/0.048 on 7-Scenes), surface normal estimation improves over StableNormal/DSine, and novel view synthesis substantially exceeds AnySplat (e.g., 20.62 vs 17.62 PSNR on RealEstate10K 2-view).

The limitations section (Sec. C) is honest, explicitly identifying poor performance on dynamic/autonomous-driving scenes and constraints on resolution and view count, and proposing concrete future directions.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited and the dependency on VGGT is under-acknowledged. The backbone, DPT heads, camera-transformer head, and even the losses are inherited ('we utilize DPT heads... following the design of VGGT'; 'we follow VGGT to implement L_cam, L_points, and L_depth'; training 'initialized from the pretrained weights of VGGT'). The principal new mechanism is tokenizing compact priors as single concatenated tokens and adding depth tokens—a fairly simple design—so the contribution is largely an integration of existing components.

There is a direct internal contradiction about the core 3DGS mechanism. Sec. 3.2 states Gaussian centers are obtained by back-projecting predicted depth using ground-truth camera poses/intrinsics, whereas Sec. A.1 states 'instead of using the depth estimated by the depth head to compute the Gaussian positions, we rely on the GS head to directly predict both the positions and other attributes,' and Table 6's ablation says positions 'are derived from the depth maps estimated by the Depth head.' These three statements cannot all be true, and the ambiguity undermines the reproducibility and interpretation of the NVS results.

Key equations contain errors that make them unusable as written. The gradient consistency loss (Eq. 11) has identical terms on both sides ($\nabla\hat{D}_i[\hat{M}_i]-\nabla\hat{D}_i[\hat{M}_i]$), so it is literally zero rather than the intended GS-depth vs. depth-head pseudo-depth consistency. Eq. 9 supervises normals but denotes the prediction as $\hat{E}_i$ (already used for cameras). These are not cosmetic; they affect whether the described training can be reproduced.

The novel-view-synthesis ablations do not support the stated conclusion. In Table 6, 'Ours' (20.29 PSNR) is statistically indistinguishable from 'w/o GT Cameras' (20.30) and 'w/o GS DPT' (20.28) on RealEstate10K, yet the text claims 'removing any component degrades novel view rendering performance.' Only the 'w/o Novel Views' variant shows a real drop. This suggests two of the three claimed design choices are inconsequential.

The prior-embedding ablation (Table 5) is over-claimed. The 'single token' advantage over dense Plücker/Raymap is marginal and mixed: for intrinsics, dense raymap actually achieves higher focal accuracy (86.48 vs 84.43), and the average gains (61.06 vs 60.44; 68.96 vs 66.58) are small. The blanket statement that 'single token offers both superior performance and high efficiency' is not fully borne out.

Potential train/test contamination is not addressed. DL3DV appears in the training-data list (Sec. A.2) and is also used as an NVS test set (Table 4), and RealEstate10K is used both for training-adjacent evaluation and testing. The paper asserts 'unseen scenes' without documenting scene-level disjointness, which is essential for the SOTA claims to be credible.

The NVS comparison may be unfair to pose-free baselines. The method back-projects Gaussians using ground-truth camera poses and intrinsics (and the strongest 'w/ intrinsics/camera pose' rows inject GT poses directly), while the main competitors (AnySplat, FLARE) are pose-free. Providing privileged calibration while comparing against uncalibrated methods inflates the apparent margin unless explicitly controlled.

The SOTA claim in the abstract is overstated relative to the evidence. On Sintel camera-pose estimation, WorldMirror (ATE 0.096, RPE trans 0.058) is clearly worse than pi3 (0.074, 0.040), and on DTU completion it is worse than pi3. The abstract's unqualified 'state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks' does not hold for all reported tasks.

Reproducibility is weak at submission time: code/models are only promised ('will be publicly available soon'), no seeds/variance/error bars are reported, and several essential components (dynamic prior injection, curriculum learning) are deferred to a brief Sec. A.2, leaving the training procedure under-specified.

strengths: The paper presents a genuinely unified feed-forward model that jointly predicts point maps, multi-view depth, camera parameters, surface normals, and 3D Gaussians, and the evaluation spans a broad set of benchmarks (7-Scenes, NRGBD, DTU, RealEstate10K, Sintel, TUM, ScanNet, NYUv2, iBims-1, DL3DV, VR-NeRF). The breadth of the empirical study is a real strength.

The multi-modal prior prompting design is well motivated and empirically validated. Table 1 and Figure 6 convincingly show that injecting a single prior improves not only the corresponding task but also other tasks, which supports the interesting claim of cross-task geometric synergy from priors.

Novel view synthesis results (Table 4) show large, consistent improvements over AnySplat across sparse- and dense-view settings (e.g., 25.14 vs 19.96 PSNR at 32 views), and the post-optimization study (Table 8) demonstrates the predicted point cloud/3DGS is a good initialization.

The prior-embedding ablation (Table 5) is a useful and somewhat counter-intuitive result: a compact single-token embedding for pose/intrinsics outperforms dense Plücker/raymap conditioning while using far fewer parameters, which is a practical and reusable finding.

The training methodology is thoughtfully engineered (dynamic prior injection by random toggling, curriculum over task/data/resolution) and the hybrid normal supervision (annotated + pseudo normals from depth) is a sensible way to exploit heterogeneous data.
weaknesses: The core novelty is incremental relative to VGGT. The architecture (DPT dense heads, transformer camera head, VGGT-style losses) is largely inherited, and the new contribution reduces to token-based encoding of priors plus random prior dropout during training. This is reasonable but modest, and the paper's framing of being a 'foundational 3D reconstruction framework' overstates the conceptual leap.

Reproducibility is a concern: code and models are only promised ('will be publicly available soon'), training requires 32 H20 GPUs, and key details live in the appendix. Additionally, Eq. 11 in the appendix contains an apparent typo — both sides of the gradient-consistency loss are identical (||∇D̂[M̂] − ∇D̂[M̂]||), so the intended consistency term is unclear and cannot be reproduced as written.

There is a potential train/test overlap: DL3DV (Ling et al., 2024) is listed among the 15 training datasets while DL3DV is also used as an NVS evaluation benchmark (Table 4). The paper follows the FLARE test split, but it does not demonstrate that this split is disjoint from the DL3DV data used for training. This should be clarified to rule out leakage.

The NVS ablation (Table 6) does not convincingly support its conclusions: 'Ours' (20.29) is essentially tied with 'w/o GT Cameras' (20.30) and 'w/o GS DPT' (20.28) on RealEstate10K (2 views), yet the text states that 'removing any component degrades' performance. The deltas are within noise and no variance/error bars are reported anywhere, weakening several 'confirms that ... are crucial' claims.

The 'state-of-the-art across tasks' claim is overstated. Camera pose estimation (Table 2) is only marginally better than π³ (99.99/95.81/86.28 vs 99.99/95.62/85.90) and worse on Sintel ATE (0.096 vs 0.074), and depth results (Table 7) are below π³ on several metrics. These are honestly acknowledged in the appendix but not reflected in the abstract/contributions.

The prior-conditioning setup is evaluated only with clean ground-truth priors. In realistic deployment priors are noisy (e.g., depth from LIDAR/RGB-D, imperfect calibration), and the paper provides no study of robustness to perturbed or noisy priors, which is central to the 'any-prior' claim. How depth is normalized to [0,1] while preserving metric scale is also under-specified.

The surface-normal gains, while consistent, are modest (e.g., ScanNet mean 13.8 vs 16.0 for StableNormal), and the attribution to 'multi-task shared representations' is not isolated from the use of additional training data and pseudo-normal supervision, so the causal claim is not fully supported.

strengths: Presents a unified feed-forward framework that flexibly accepts optional geometric priors (intrinsics, camera poses, depth) and simultaneously predicts point maps, depth, surface normals, camera parameters, and 3D Gaussians in a single pass, which is a practically useful direction.

The Multi-modal Tokenization design is simple and effective: global priors (poses, intrinsics) are encoded as single tokens and concatenated, while dense depth is added to image tokens. Ablations show this is more efficient and often more accurate than dense per-pixel embeddings.

Extensive empirical evaluation across many tasks and benchmarks: point map reconstruction (7-Scenes, NRGBD, DTU), camera pose estimation (RealEstate10K, Sintel, TUM-dynamics), surface normals (ScanNet, NYUv2, iBims-1), novel view synthesis (DL3DV, RealEstate10K, VR-NeRF, MatrixCity), and depth (NYUv2, Sintel, KITTI). The no-prior WorldMirror already surpasses VGGT and π3 on point map reconstruction and is competitive on camera pose estimation.

Thorough ablation studies cover prior embedding strategies, novel-view-synthesis design choices, curriculum versus joint training, prior dropout probability, robustness to noisy priors, depth injection/normalization, GPU memory, maximum view counts, and inference speed.

Reproducibility details are strong: 15 training datasets, loss formulations and weights, optimization settings, hardware (32 H20 GPUs), training time (~70 hours), inference times, and memory consumption are reported. Code and model weights are claimed to be publicly available.

The paper includes an honest limitations section acknowledging poor performance on dynamic scenes and driving environments, constraints on input resolution and view count, and high memory usage for the 3DGS head. It also includes an ethics/impact statement discussing privacy and misuse concerns.
weaknesses: The abstract claims state-of-the-art performance on depth and camera estimation, but the evidence does not fully support this: in Table 7, π3 outperforms WorldMirror on Sintel and KITTI depth metrics, and in Table 2, WorldMirror is worse than π3 and VGGT on Sintel camera ATE/RPE. These overclaims should be qualified.

Several comparisons are not apples-to-apples: WorldMirror is evaluated with ground-truth priors (intrinsics, poses, depth) against baselines that receive no priors (e.g., Tables 1–3). Although the no-prior WorldMirror results are also reported, the highlighted prior-conditioned results can mislead readers about the magnitude of the method's advantage. Fair comparisons against prior-guided methods (Pow3R, MapAnything) are limited mainly to Fig. 5 for point maps.

DL3DV is included in the training data (Sec. A.2), yet the novel-view-synthesis evaluation on DL3DV is described as 'zero-shot' (Sec. B.2). This is inaccurate: DL3DV results are within-dataset and do not demonstrate zero-shot generalization. The zero-shot claim should be restricted to datasets not used in training (e.g., RealEstate10K, VR-NeRF, MatrixCity).

The surface normal comparison in Table 3 is ambiguous: WorldMirror is compared to monocular normal estimators (DSine, StableNormal, GeoWizard, etc.), but the paper does not specify whether WorldMirror uses single-view or multi-view inputs for this benchmark. If multi-view inputs are used, the comparison is not directly fair and should be clarified.

There are mathematical and notation errors that undermine soundness. Eq. 9 defines the consistency loss as ||∇\hat{D}_i[\hat{M}_i] − ∇\hat{D}_i[\hat{M}_i]||, which is identically zero; it likely should involve the depth-head prediction \tilde{D}_i. Eq. 7 says it supervises \hat{E}_i but should be \hat{N}_i. The description of Gaussian position prediction is also contradictory: it first says positions are computed from predicted depths and ground-truth camera parameters, then says the GS head predicts positions independently.

The novelty is incremental: the architecture builds heavily on VGGT, uses standard token concatenation/addition and DPT decoders, and adds a 3DGS head with sequential fine-tuning. Concurrent works such as MapAnything and OmniVGGT already explore prior conditioning. The 'first' claim needs careful qualification, and the technical contribution is primarily a well-executed combination of existing ideas.

The claim that 'prior injection yields universal gains across all tasks' is not deeply analyzed. Since the model is explicitly trained with prior dropout to use such inputs, improved performance when priors are supplied at inference is expected. The paper would benefit from stronger analysis of why gains transfer across tasks and whether they stem from genuine shared representation learning rather than simply from additional conditioning information.
The abstract states that code and model weights are publicly available but no URL is provided in the manuscript, which limits reproducibility verification at review time.

strengths: The paper presents a genuinely comprehensive unified system, evaluating the same feed-forward model across an unusually broad set of tasks (point maps, camera pose, monocular/video depth, surface normals, NVS, surface reconstruction) and many datasets (Tables 1-4, 7-11), which is more than most single-task papers attempt.

Several results are strong and well-supported: point map reconstruction with all priors (Table 1: 0.018 Acc on 7-Scenes, 0.735 on DTU) and surface normal estimation (Table 3: 13.8 mean on ScanNet, 15.1 on NYUv2) clearly beat prior methods.

The empirical study is thorough, including prior-embedding ablations (Table 5), NVS design ablations (Table 6), curriculum-vs-joint training (Table 13), dropout sensitivity (Table 14), depth-injection strategy (Table 15), depth normalization (Table 16), and robustness to noisy priors (Table 12).

Reproducibility is handled reasonably well: code and weights are released, training data/GPUs, learning rates, loss weights, wall-clock time, memory (Table 17), max-view (Table 18), and inference latency (Table 19) are all reported.
The robustness analysis under noisy poses/intrinsics/depth (Table 12) and the depth-normalization ablation (Table 16) provide useful, non-obvious insights about prior conditioning.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and incremental. The architecture is explicitly built on VGGT ('Inspired by the architecture used in VGGT'; 'initialized from the pretrained weights of VGGT'), and prior injection is already established by Pow3R, MapAnything, and OmniVGGT (acknowledged as concurrent). The claimed 'core designs' (single-token concatenation for poses/intrinsics, element-wise addition for depth, and curriculum learning) are straightforward combinations rather than fundamentally new mechanisms.

The central NVS comparisons are confounded. The authors themselves state the improvement 'likely stems from a combination of our unified architecture and the broader training data scale,' so the SOTA claim cannot be cleanly attributed to the method. This is an important evidential weakness for a paper whose headline contribution is unified prior-aware prediction.

Several headline claims are overstated relative to the tables. The abstract/intro claim to 'significantly exceed' AnySplat in NVS, yet in Table 4 WorldMirror has worse LPIPS at 24 views (0.241 vs 0.221) and 64 views (0.239 vs 0.208). Camera-pose claims of superiority are contradicted by Sintel, where π3 is better on ATE (0.074 vs 0.096), RPE-trans (0.040 vs 0.058), and RPE-rot (0.282 vs 0.490).

Many improvements are marginal. In Table 1 the no-prior WorldMirror vs π3 differences are tiny (7-Scenes Acc 0.043 vs 0.048; NRGBD 0.041 vs 0.026). In Table 6, 'Ours' vs 'w/o GT Cameras' is 20.29 vs 20.30 on RealEstate10K, i.e., within noise, weakening the claim that the design is 'essential for optimal performance.'

The 'universal gains from prior injection' claim is partly trivial (providing ground-truth poses/intrinsics/depth naturally helps) and partly marginal, so it does not by itself demonstrate an emergent synergy as strongly as asserted.

The comparison to prior-guided methods Pow3R and MapAnything is relegated to a figure (Fig. 5) with vague language ('outperforms both methods across most conditions'); no numeric tables or per-dataset breakdowns are provided, and Pow3R is manually extended to multi-view by the authors, which may not be a fair comparison.

The 3DGS rendering uses ground-truth camera parameters, and NVS training relies on GT poses, which limits the 'pose-free' framing; the dependence on GT poses for supervision and rendering is a notable caveat that is not fully reconciled with the pose-free positioning.

Presentation contains careless errors: Eq. 9 is ill-formed (∇D̂_i[M̂_i] − ∇D̂_i[M̂_i], identical terms), Eq. 2 references T̂_i^img rather than features, equations are duplicated/numbered inconsistently (Eqs. 3 and 4), and reference years are frequently wrong (e.g., Matterport3D cited as 2024 but is 2017; ScanNet cited as 2023 but is 2017; Fast3R listed under 2024 vs 2025). These suggest insufficient proofreading.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely useful problem—unifying flexible geometric prior conditioning (intrinsics, poses, depth) with comprehensive multi-task 3D output (point maps, depth, normals, cameras, 3DGS)—within a single feed-forward model. This is a broader scope than either Pow3R (priors only) or VGGT (multi-task only), and the framing of these two capabilities as mutually reinforcing is a coherent and valuable research direction.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad and covers five distinct task families (point map reconstruction, camera pose estimation, surface normals, novel view synthesis, depth) on many benchmarks (7-Scenes, NRGBD, DTU, RealEstate10K, Sintel, TUM, ScanNet, NYUv2, iBims-1, DL3DV, VR-NeRF, MatrixCity). State-of-the-art or competitive results are reported across nearly all of them, and the prior-injection tables (Tab. 1, Tab. 9, Fig. 7) consistently show that adding priors improves not only the corresponding task but also other tasks, which substantiates the central synergy claim.

The ablation study on prior embedding (Tab. 5) is informative: the single-token approach beats dense Plücker/raymap embeddings while using ~6-8x fewer extra parameters, and the depth injection ablation (Tab. 15) shows addition is both cheaper (1.14 vs 1.74 TFLOPs) and marginally better than concatenation. The robustness study to noisy priors (Tab. 12) and the dropout sensitivity analysis (Tab. 14) are thoughtful additions that increase confidence in practical usefulness.

Efficiency and practicality are addressed carefully, with GPU-memory scaling (Tab. 17), maximum view counts (Tab. 18), inference latency against VGGT/Pi3 (Tab. 19), and a modular on-demand 3DGS head. The observation that prior injection adds negligible latency (WorldMirror-Geo matches VGGT) is a useful result.

Reproducibility is taken seriously in intent: code and weights are stated to be released, training losses and weights are specified (Eqs. 4-9, Sec. A.2), and the 15-dataset training mixture and two-stage schedule are documented. The limitations section (Sec. G) honestly discusses dynamic-scene and long-sequence weaknesses.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental and heavily reliant on VGGT. The backbone (global-local attention), DPT decoders, and multi-task heads are adopted from VGGT, and the model is initialized from VGGT pretrained weights (Sec. 3.2, Sec. A.2). The actual contributions reduce to (i) tokenizing priors and (ii) adding a normal head and a 3DGS head. The paper itself acknowledges concurrent prior-conditioning works (MapAnything's unified additive priors, OmniVGGT's zero-convolution adapters), and the distinction from these is not convincingly established beyond a single-token-vs-dense ablation.

The 'unified end-to-end' framing is partly undercut by the decoupled sequential training: the GS head is trained with all other parameters frozen (Sec. 3.2), and 3DGS rendering uses ground-truth camera parameters rather than predicted ones (Sec. 3.2, Tab. 6). This means the model is not truly jointly optimized for appearance and geometry, and pose-free NVS rendering quality is not demonstrated. The 'one-for-all' claim should be tempered accordingly.

A data-scale confound weakens the central NVS claim. The paper admits (Sec. 5.1) that gains over DepthSplat may stem from 'the broader training data scale' (15 datasets). No controlled experiment (e.g., matching training data or fine-tuning baselines on the same mixture) is provided, so the architectural contribution to NVS quality is not isolated. Similarly, the strong surface-normal results over specialized methods (StableNormal, GeoWizard) could be driven by the large pseudo-normal-augmented data rather than the architecture.

Several NVS comparisons appear to use different resolutions and protocols across methods (Tab. 4: 448x252 vs 256x256; Tab. 9: 518x378; Tab. 11: 256x256 with cropping). The 'WorldMirror*' row in Tab. 4 uses pose-free optimization (Ye et al., 2024a) to align with baselines, which complicates a clean architectural comparison. The ablation in Tab. 6 is also weak—'w/o GS DPT' and 'w/o GT Cameras' are within noise of the full model on several metrics (e.g., RealEstate10K PSNR 20.28 vs 20.29; DL3DV LPIPS 0.218 vs 0.198), so the design choices are not strongly justified by the evidence.

The curriculum/decoupled-vs-joint comparison (Tab. 13) is run only for 32,500 steps 'under time constraints,' which is a much shorter schedule than the final model (150 epochs on 32 H20 GPUs). It is unclear whether the joint-training baseline would close the gap with full training, so the claim that joint training is fundamentally inferior is not firmly established.

Some table entries are anomalous and under-explained: in Tab. 1 (DTU), the camera-pose prior (0.990) is worse than the depth prior (0.831) and barely better than no prior (1.017), and combining pose+intrinsics+depth (0.735) is only marginally better than depth alone—yet the text claims pose priors 'capture global geometry.' The relative contributions of priors across datasets are inconsistent and not analyzed.

Reproducibility is limited in practice: the code/weights URL is blank in the abstract, training requires 32 H20 GPUs for ~70 hours (~2,240 GPU-hours), and key preprocessing details (how GT normals/depth/poses are derived and harmonized across the 15 heterogeneous datasets, and how pseudo-normals from plane fitting are validated) are omitted.
